# Can an Aspect Ratio Shift Affect Your Differential?

Swapping from a 255/65R17 tire to a 265/70R17 on a midsize rear-wheel-drive pickup is a common modification, but the resulting geometry change demands scrutiny. You noted a circumference difference of roughly 124mm between the two sets. This isn't merely cosmetic; it fundamentally alters the relationship between wheel rotation and vehicle travel, introducing immediate stress into the drivetrain components, specifically the differential.

The core issue is axle speed variance. In a standard open differential, the output shafts rotate at the same speed when the vehicle moves straight. However, tires on the same axle must ideally cover the exact same distance per revolution to maintain this balance. By increasing the overall diameter (achieved here by widening the width from 255mm to 265mm and increasing the aspect ratio from 65% to 70%), you effectively lengthen the tire's rolling circumference.

If your new tires are mounted on one axle while keeping the original setup on the opposite axle, or if this is part of a mixed fleet scenario where other wheels remain stock, the drivetrain encounters conflicting rotational demands. The differential will attempt to average out these speeds, but because the physical distance covered per turn differs by over 10%, the internal gears face immediate torque bias issues. In an open differential, power naturally flows to the wheel with least resistance. If one wheel is effectively "larger" due to incorrect sizing relative to the other, the system compensates by allowing the smaller effective tire to spin faster or slower than intended, causing the larger tire to slip or drag against the pavement.

When this mismatch occurs on a rear-wheel-drive platform, the vehicle's computer systems often detect the anomaly immediately. Modern ECUs rely on wheel speed sensors to calculate ABS braking points and traction control interventions. A 124mm circumference discrepancy creates a velocity error that the system interprets as a wheel slipping or losing traction. Consequently, you will likely see the "Traction Control" or "ABS" warning lights illuminate intermittently during acceleration or cornering. The ECU attempts to correct this by applying brake pressure to specific wheels or limiting engine torque, effectively throttling performance and altering the driving dynamics in unintended ways.

If the modification was intended to be symmetricalâmeaning all four tires were swapped to the new 265/70R17 sizeâthe differential itself might mechanically survive the change without grinding gears, provided the slip angles remain within design tolerances. However, the calibration of your vehicle's electronic stability control (ESC) and transmission shift points will now be based on incorrect wheel speed data. The transmission may upshift too early or downshift aggressively because it thinks the car is moving faster than it actually is relative to the sensor inputs.

From a mechanical engineering standpoint, even with all four tires swapped, the final drive ratio remains unchanged. The differential gears are sized for the original torque delivery based on the original gear inches. While the physical stress on the pinion and ring gears doesn't immediately increase in a linear fashion simply because the tire is wider, the change in effective gearing alters the engine's RPM at any given road speed. This shifts the power band, potentially placing higher loads on the drivetrain during low-speed torque delivery if the engine is forced to work harder to compensate for the changed ratio.

The 124mm increase you calculated translates to a significant percentage jump in diameter. For context, this is roughly a 5-6% increase in overall diameter depending on the original rolling radius. In automotive engineering, deviations beyond 3% usually trigger electronic warnings and require recalibration of the vehicle's control modules. Without performing an ECU reflash or wheel speed sensor calibration to account for the new tire size, the mismatch between mechanical reality and digital perception creates a hostile environment for your differential and ABS system.

If you are managing a fleet of vehicles or building a custom build where precise data logging is required, such discrepancies invalidate telemetry data. You cannot trust wheel-speed-based calculations for range estimation or speed accuracy. The safest technical approach is to ensure all four wheels match exactly in diameter, width, and offset, or to revert to the original specifications if electronic integration becomes too complex to manage manually.
